opus-5.5.text:
I think part of it is just that alignment is still a very young field. We don't have a settled paradigm yet, so we don't actually know which skills and perspectives will turn out to matter most. When a field is that early, you want a lot of different people trying a lot of different angles, because the approach that ends up working might come from somewhere nobody expected.

There's also something specific about the problem itself. Alignment isn't purely a machine learning problem. Yes, a lot of the day-to-day work is empirical ML research: training models, running experiments, building evaluations. But underneath that there are questions about what it even means for a system to do what we want, how humans give feedback, what our values actually are, how you supervise something that might be smarter than you in some domains. Those questions touch philosophy, cognitive science, economics, even things like how organizations and institutions make decisions. People who come from those backgrounds often notice things that someone who has only ever trained neural networks might miss.

And honestly, I've seen it work in practice. Some of the people I've worked with who've been most effective didn't follow the traditional path of a PhD in machine learning. Some came from physics, some from software engineering, some were basically self-taught. What they had in common was that they cared a lot about the problem, they were willing to get their hands dirty, and they could learn quickly. The ML tooling has gotten good enough, and the research is empirical enough, that if you're a strong engineer and a clear thinker, you can get up to speed surprisingly fast.

The other thing I'd say is that groupthink is a real risk. If everyone working on alignment has the same training and reads the same papers, you can end up with a lot of shared blind spots. You get collective confidence about assumptions that haven't really been tested. Having people who ask the "naive" questions, the ones insiders stopped asking a long time ago, is actually really valuable. Sometimes the naive question is the one that reveals the whole approach is built on something shaky.

So for anyone listening who's thinking, "I don't have the right credentials for this," I'd really encourage them not to rule themselves out. The field needs more people, and it needs different kinds of people. What matters most is whether you can make progress on hard problems, and that shows up in a lot of different backgrounds.

r001.rationale: The response says alignment is not purely a machine learning problem and names related questions and fields beyond ML.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think the honest starting point is that we don't actually know how to solve alignment yet. If we did, this would be a very different conversation. And when you're working on a problem where the solution isn't known, where the field is still arguing about what the right framing even is, you really don't want everyone approaching it from the same angle. If you hire fifty people who all did the same ML PhD under similar advisors and read the same papers, you get fifty people who share the same blind spots. They'll all miss the same things, and they'll all be confident about the same wrong assumptions.

So part of it is just epistemic hygiene. Alignment touches on a lot of things that aren't core machine learning. There are questions about what it means to specify what we want, which is sort of a philosophy problem. There are questions about how you evaluate systems that might be smarter than you in some domain, which borrows from how we think about auditing, or from how scientists trust each other's results, or from how institutions deal with principal-agent problems. There's a lot of empirical, almost experimental-psychology-flavored work in understanding how models behave. People who come in from economics, or from security, or from neuroscience, or who've just spent years building real systems in industry, they bring intuitions that a pure ML researcher often doesn't have.

The other thing I'd say is that I've been surprised quite a few times by where good ideas come from. Some of the most useful contributions I've seen came from people who didn't have the standard credentials, who maybe taught themselves, or switched careers fairly late, or came from a totally different discipline. They asked questions that sounded naive at first, and then turned out to be pointing at something the rest of us had just stopped noticing. If the field had a very narrow gate, those people wouldn't have been in the room.

And then practically, there just aren't enough people working on this. The problem is big and the number of people seriously working on it is still small relative to how much is at stake. So if you insist on a very traditional profile, you're throwing away a lot of talent for no good reason. What I actually care about is whether someone can think clearly, whether they're willing to engage with the hard parts rather than route around them, and whether they can learn fast. Those traits are pretty orthogonal to what your degree says.

I'd add one caveat, which is that diversity of background isn't a substitute for rigor. You still need people to actually understand the technical details and to be able to run real experiments or make precise arguments. But I've found that motivated people from other fields pick that up faster than you'd expect, and the reverse, getting a narrowly trained researcher to suddenly see the problem from a new angle, is often harder.

r001.rationale: The candidate says alignment involves questions beyond core machine learning and gives examples from philosophy, auditing, science, institutions, and experimental psychology.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that we don’t really know what the solution to alignment looks like. We have a number of ideas, but there’s a lot of uncertainty about which approaches will work, and there are probably useful approaches that we haven’t thought of yet. If everyone has similar training and similar intuitions, they’re more likely to make the same assumptions and miss the same things.

People from different backgrounds can bring different tools, ask different questions, or notice that something we’ve been taking for granted isn’t actually obvious. And that’s particularly valuable in a field where framing the problem well is a big part of the work.

That doesn’t mean every different perspective is equally useful. You still want people who can reason carefully, learn the technical details, and test their ideas. But I wouldn’t want to use a conventional career path as a proxy for those abilities. Someone who took an unusual route might have exactly the insight we’re missing.

r001.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty, varied tools, and different backgrounds, but does not identify that AI alignment includes many aspects beyond machine learning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main reason is that we don’t really know what the solution to alignment looks like. If we knew exactly what needed to be done, we could hire people who were very good at doing that particular thing. But we’re still figuring out which questions to ask, which assumptions are wrong, and which approaches might work.

So if everyone has a similar background, they might all be very capable, but they’re also more likely to share blind spots. Someone coming from a different field might ask a question that seems naive at first, but actually exposes an assumption that nobody has properly justified. Or they might bring a way of thinking about the problem that we wouldn’t otherwise have considered.

That doesn’t mean that every different perspective is equally useful. You still want people who can think clearly, learn quickly, and test their ideas. But I wouldn’t want us to confuse having a conventional machine learning background with having the ability to make progress on alignment.

r001.rationale: The response values different backgrounds and says a conventional machine learning background is not required for progress, but it does not identify that AI alignment has many aspects beyond machine learning.
